articles.title: The flag file my watchdog wrote was 0 bytes, so the alert fired for 8 days
articles.excerpt: A monitoring script is supposed to stop shouting once you've been told. Mine shouted every morning for eight days, and the reason was a file with zero bytes. The pattern is common: a cron job runs eve…
articles.body: A monitoring script is supposed to stop shouting once you've been told. Mine shouted every morning for eight days, and the reason was a file with zero bytes. The design that looked fine The pattern is common: a cron job runs every hour, checks something, and when the check fails it sends a message. To avoid a message every hour, it keeps a latch — a small JSON file with the date of the last time it warned. If the latch says "already warned today", the job stays quiet. def already_warned ( chave ) : try : with open ( LATCH ) as fh : dados = json . load ( fh ) return dados . get ( chave ) == today ( ) except FileNotFoundError : return False except Exception : return False # <-- the line that cost me 8 days Note the last branch. It exists "to avoid crashing the monitor".
articles.author: SAMUELFMEDEIROS

articles.title: Building Signal2Speech: answering questions with an EEG headset at Hack the Nest 2026 (Update 1)
articles.excerpt: Note: This is only the first of many updates. We will also include a final post which will summarize the whole event. We are Order of the Golden Eagles, a team of four at Hack the Nest 2026 (Eastern M…
articles.body: Note: This is only the first of many updates. We will also include a final post which will summarize the whole event. We are Order of the Golden Eagles, a team of four at Hack the Nest 2026 (Eastern Michigan University), and we are building Signal2Speech. It is an accessibility prototype for people who have difficulty speaking or typing. A conversation partner asks a question, the app offers a few short replies, and the person wearing an EEG headset (a cap that reads electrical activity from the brain) picks, previews, and confirms the words they want spoken. Our main rule is that the app suggests what to say, but the wearer decides what actually gets said. We are about five and a half hours in. This post covers where the project stands and a few things we ran into along the way.

articles.title: Your CI artifacts and preview deployments can leak unprotected JavaScript
articles.excerpt: Many teams start obfuscating or VM-protecting client JavaScript in the production Vite or webpack build, then assume the problem is solved. The production CDN may be clean. Meanwhile, the unprotected…
articles.body: Many teams start obfuscating or VM-protecting client JavaScript in the production Vite or webpack build, then assume the problem is solved. The production CDN may be clean. Meanwhile, the unprotected bundle is sitting in a CI artifact, a preview URL, a GitHub Actions zip retained for 90 days, or a leftover object from last week's deploy. This article is about the places unprotected JavaScript escapes after you "turned protection on," and how to close those holes without making pull-request previews useless.

articles.body: Corevia 4.0 Is Here: Building Reliable Applications Beyond Traditional PHP Frameworks Corevia V4.0.0 is now available on GitHub. After building the foundations across Corevia V1, V2, and V3, I'm excited to share the next major milestone of the project. Corevia is an open-source, modular PHP application framework and runtime designed around a simple principle: Modern applications need more than routes, controllers, and database queries. They need reliable execution, clear boundaries, and the flexibility to integrate multiple technologies without unnecessary complexity. Version 4 extends that vision with safer application upgrades, stronger data and identity capabilities, durable operations, optional AI infrastructure, and improved cross-runtime integration.

articles.title: Electron Internationalization: A Practical Guide to Locale Detection, Message Formatting, RTL, and Runtime Language Switching
articles.excerpt: Most Electron apps are built in one language, and the first internationalization pass usually means dropping a few translated strings into the renderer. That works until you ship to a non-English user…
articles.body: Most Electron apps are built in one language, and the first internationalization pass usually means dropping a few translated strings into the renderer. That works until you ship to a non-English user: the menu bar and native dialogs stay English, dates and currency render in the wrong format, plurals break for languages with more than two forms, and a right-to-left locale leaves the layout mirrored only halfway. Desktop i18n is broader than web i18n because an Electron app owns the shell — the main process, the tray, the application menu, native dialogs, and every renderer window — and each surface reads its own strings.

articles.excerpt: On Episode 236 of This Week In Space, Tariq Malik and Rod Pyle are joined by Mikhail Tikhonov to talk about how life can take more unusual forms, ones we might not even recognize.
articles.body: On Episode 236 of This Week In Space , Tariq Malik and Rod Pyle are joined by Mikhail Tikhonov to talk about how life can take more unusual forms, ones we might not even recognize. When we think of extraterrestrials, our minds generally go from the latex-suited bipedal aliens seen in Star Trek and Star Wars to more exotic critters in sci-fi movies. Scientists think in terms of carbon-based microbial life and other lower life forms. But some researchers, such as Tikhonov from Washington University, suggest that life can take more unusual forms, ones we might not even recognize. He further suggests a new definition of life: something that takes in and transforms energy and replicates. His ideas radically expand our notions of alien life and how it might be recognized.

articles.excerpt: SpaceX is looking into why its latest Starship megarocket test flight missed the first of two planned landings on Friday (Nov. 13) during the Starship Flight 15 test.
articles.body: Update for 3:40 p.m. ET on Nov. 14: SpaceX's Kate Tice provided more information about the booster abort at about 3:30 p.m. EST (1830 GMT) on Nov. 14, during the company's Flight 15 webcast. "Early indications are that the booster ended its boostback [burn] early due to a low fuel mass alarm," she said. "The team is still investigating the root cause on that." SpaceX is looking into why its latest Starship megarocket test flight missed the first of two planned landings on Friday (Nov. 13), triggering an automatic abort that destroyed the booster. The giant Starship rocket , a massive two-stage vehicle that's the largest launcher on Earth, soared into orbit from SpaceX's Starbase in South Texas on Friday on the company's ambitious Flight 15 test flight.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 14, 1969: NASA's Apollo 12 astronauts launch to the moon on a 'pinpoint landing' lunar mission
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 14, 1969, the Apollo 12 astronauts launched to the moon. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 14, 1969, the Apollo 12 mission launched to the moon. This was the second moon landing of the Apollo program. The two astronauts on board were Pete Conrad , commander, and Alan Bean , the lunar module pilot. Astronaut Richard Gordon , the command module pilot, stayed in the command module and orbited the moon while his crewmates went to the surface. The astronauts made a pinpoint landing in a lunar mare called the Ocean of Storms. The previous moon mission, Apollo 11 , drifted far from the planned landing zone. But Apollo 12 landed close to a scientific target. That target was a robotic lander called Surveyor 3 . Scientists wanted to look at Surveyor 3 to see how well the spacecraft lasted on the moon since it landed there more than two years earlier.

articles.title: 'Now everything changes': SpaceX catches Starship upper stage for 1st time ever (video)
articles.excerpt: SpaceX caught the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever today (Nov. 14), a landmark achievement that could unlock the giant vehicle's immense potential.
articles.body: SpaceX caught the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever today (Nov. 14), a landmark achievement that could unlock the giant vehicle's immense potential. Starship launched on its 15th test flight on Friday evening (Nov. 13), rising into the sky from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas. The mission plan called for bringing both of the vehicle's stages back to Starbase and catching them with the launch tower's "chopstick" arms — an unprecedented total recovery of an orbital rocket . That didn't happen; Starship's Super Heavy booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But Ship succeeded in its attempt, notching a huge milestone for SpaceX and its dream of full rocket reuse.
